Abstract

Autonomous agents have long served as a central pillar in the pursuit of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), yet traditional approaches are often limited by isolated training environments and simplistic policy functions that diverge from human learning. By utilizing web-scale knowledge, Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a powerful foundation for building human-level autonomous agentic systems. This seminar delivers a systematic review of LLM-based autonomous agents from a unified architectural perspective, focusing on four core functional modules: profiling, memory, planning, and action. The discussion surveys diverse multi-agent applications across social sciences, natural sciences (automated chemical synthesis), and software engineering workflows. Additionally, it explores current objective and subjective evaluation strategies, ranging from human Turing tests to simulated multi-task benchmarking environments. Based on an extensive review, the seminar highlights open research challenges, including prompt robustness, generalized human alignment boundaries, and the transition toward mechanism engineering, providing critical insights into the future of self-driven evolutionary AI.

Abstract

The rapid deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) across multi-domain software interfaces has transformed human-computer interaction, but it also introduces critical system vulnerabilities and security risks. This seminar examines the security landscape of using LLMs, with a particular emphasis on the distinct complexities of conversational models like ChatGPT. The discussion provides a holistic overview of current research categorized into five major threat vectors: structural token bias, automated disinformation generation, behavioral misuse across educational and corporate frameworks, adversarial attacks, and training data privacy violations.
